claims.text: The initial material consists of nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
High grain-boundary density influences defect mobility and diffusion kinetics.
Local lattice distortions influence defect mobility and diffusion kinetics.
Local lattice distortions in a high-entropy solid solution create a rough atomic energy landscape.
The rough energy landscape produced by local lattice distortions slows atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion promotes defect recombination.
Slower atomic diffusion retards elemental segregation and stabilizes the solid-solution phase.
Nanoparticles with high grain-boundary density can maintain structural and chemical stability up to 1923 K.
At sufficiently high temperature, thermally activated diffusion can overcome the proposed kinetic barriers.
Elevated-temperature exposure can lead to elemental segregation and precipitate formation.
Nanoparticles with fewer grain boundaries will undergo phase separation more rapidly than nanoparticles with high grain-boundary density.
High-grain-boundary-density nanoparticles will retain a uniform solid solution with minimal precipitation throughout 473–1923 K.
Larger-grained nanoparticles will develop detectable compositional inhomogeneities and secondary phases above approximately 1000 K.
Oxidation, reaction intermediates, applied electrical fields, and uncontrolled coarsening can alter the predicted stability thresholds.
Equivalent stability in high- and low-grain-boundary-density samples, or greater segregation in the high-density sample, would falsify the proposed grain-boundary-mediated stabilization mechanism.
